summary.text: A 37-year old female with type II diabetes on insulin presented with generalised body swelling for 2 months and epigastric pain for 10 days, with a history of jaundice 2 months earlier. Examination showed icterus, bilateral pitting oedema, abdominal distension, hepatomegaly and splenomegaly, with a GCS of 14/15.

Laboratory tests showed raised ALT and AST, total bilirubin 16.10 mg/dl, albumin 2.4 g/dl and INR 1.58, with negative viral and most autoimmune serology but positive anti-smooth muscle antibody. Imaging showed absent right portal vein branch flow, collaterals and splenomegaly. Liver biopsy showed bridging fibrosis with nodules, interface hepatitis and feathery degeneration.

Based on the biopsy findings she was diagnosed with autoimmune hepatitis type I and given IV ceftriaxone and prednisolone for the initial 4 days. She then developed low blood pressure, low urine output and altered sensorium suggestive of shock and was transferred to intensive care, where IV meropenem was given with nil per oral and a nasogastric tube.

She became decompensated and disoriented, developed bilateral pneumonia and remained hypotensive despite inotropes, progressing to septic shock. She died after 15 days of hospital stay; the authors attribute the demise to liver cirrhosis that followed autoimmune hepatitis, and note she did not respond to prednisolone from the initial stage.
